title: The original Gerry-mander was a state senate district
text: The word 'gerrymander' comes from a Massachusetts state senate district in Essex County, created by a redistricting act Governor Elbridge Gerry signed on February 11, 1812, and drawn as a salamander-like monster in the Boston Gazette on March 26, 1812. It was not a congressional district. This map shows the 20 congressional districts Massachusetts used for the 13th Congress, elected later in 1812.

title: Connecticut's general ticket
text: Connecticut elected all seven of its representatives statewide: each voter could vote for a candidate for every one of the seven seats. The state used this 'general ticket' from 1789 until 1837, when it switched to single-member districts. In the 13th Congress, Delaware, Georgia, New Hampshire, Rhode Island and Vermont also elected their whole delegations at large.

title: Defying the 1842 districting law
text: The Apportionment Act of 1842 required representatives to be elected 'by districts composed of contiguous territory', no district electing more than one member. Georgia, Mississippi, Missouri and New Hampshire elected their members at large anyway. The House's Committee of Elections called the districting requirement unconstitutional, and the House voted 127 to 57 to seat the members.

title: Mississippi's 'shoestring' district
text: For the 1876 election, Mississippi's Democratic legislature redrew Representative John R. Lynch's district, packing most of the state's Republican voters into a 'shoestring district' that narrowly hugged the Mississippi River. Lynch, a Black Republican, lost to Democrat James R. Chalmers, who was credited with 56 percent of the vote; the House Committee on Elections rejected Lynch's challenge.

title: The Delta in one district
text: Beginning with the 1882 election, Mississippi placed the Yazoo-Mississippi Delta, the region with the state's largest Black population, in a single congressional district. Republican Elza Jeffords won this 3rd district in 1882.

title: South Carolina's 'Black district'
text: South Carolina's 1882 map was designed to pack as many Black voters as possible into one district. The 7th snaked across the state through parts of nine counties, from the Savannah River to Winyah Bay, bypassing the city of Charleston; about 31,000 of its 38,000 voters were Black. Republican Edmund Mackey won it in 1882, and after his death Robert Smalls won it in 1884.

title: Pennsylvania's four at-large members
text: The 1911 apportionment raised Pennsylvania from 32 to 36 seats. The state kept its 32 existing districts and elected the four new members statewide, so every Pennsylvanian voted for one district member and four at-large members. Pennsylvania elected at-large members until 1923.

title: Wood v. Broom: the standards lapse
text: Mississippi's 1932 law divided the state into seven districts, and a voter sued, citing the 1911 Act's rule of compact, contiguous districts with as nearly as practicable equal populations. In Wood v. Broom (1932) the Supreme Court held that those requirements 'expired by their own limitation' with the 1911 apportionment, and that the 1929 Act contained no such provision. Congress did not restore a population standard; the courts later imposed one in 1964.

title: Minnesota: a veto forces at-large elections
text: Minnesota fell from 10 seats to 9 after the 1930 Census. The governor vetoed the legislature's new map, and in Smiley v. Holm (1932) the Supreme Court held that congressional maps are subject to the governor's veto like other laws. With no valid map, all nine members were elected at large in 1932.

title: Missouri elects 13 members statewide
text: Missouri fell from 16 seats to 13. Its governor vetoed the redistricting bill, and in Carroll v. Becker (1932) the Supreme Court, following Smiley v. Holm, held the map invalid. All 13 members were elected at large in 1932, the largest at-large delegation on this map.

title: Virginia's map struck three weeks before the election
text: Virginia had to fit ten districts into nine. Its 1932 map gave the 7th district about 337,000 people and the 8th about 184,000, and the state's Supreme Court of Appeals invalidated it three weeks before the November election. Twenty-four candidates ran statewide for the nine seats; all nine winners were Democrats.

title: Georgia's 5th and Wesberry v. Sanders
text: Georgia's 5th district (Fulton, DeKalb and Rockdale counties, including Atlanta) had 823,680 residents in 1960, while the 9th had 272,154 and the state's districts averaged 394,312. In Wesberry v. Sanders (1964), brought by 5th-district voters, the Supreme Court held that the Constitution requires congressional districts to be as nearly equal in population as practicable.

title: Dallas: the most populous district
text: Texas' 5th district, Dallas County, had 951,527 residents in 1960, the most of any district used in the 1962 elections. Texas' 4th district had 216,371, less than a quarter as many. Texas also elected one member at large, for the seat it gained after the 1960 Census.

title: Michigan's 16th vs. 12th
text: Michigan's 16th district, in the Detroit area, had 802,994 residents in 1960; its 12th, in the western Upper Peninsula, had 177,431, the smallest district in the country. Michigan also elected one member at large, for the seat it gained after the 1960 Census.

title: Alabama elects all eight at large
text: Alabama fell from nine seats to eight after the 1960 Census and was the only one of 16 states losing seats that did not redistrict. In 1962 all eight members were elected statewide. (The source shapefiles have no Alabama file for this Congress; the outline shown is the state boundary.)

title: Montana loses its second seat
text: The 1990 apportionment cost Montana one of its two seats, leaving a single district of 803,655 people, 231,189 more than the ideal district of 572,466. Montana sued, but in Department of Commerce v. Montana (1992) the Supreme Court upheld the method of equal proportions. Incumbents Pat Williams and Ron Marlenee then ran against each other; Williams won.

title: North Carolina's 12th and Shaw v. Reno
text: Drawn as North Carolina's second majority-Black district, the 12th was about 160 miles long and, for much of its length, no wider than the I-85 corridor; it was about 57 percent Black. In Shaw v. Reno (1993) the Supreme Court held that a plan so irregular it can be understood only as an effort to separate voters by race can be challenged under the Equal Protection Clause. In Shaw v. Hunt (1996) the Court struck the district down.

title: Illinois' 4th: the 'earmuffs'
text: To create a Hispanic-majority district in Chicago, the 1990s map joined the Mexican-American neighborhoods of Pilsen and Little Village on the south side with Puerto Rican Humboldt Park on the north side, linked by a thin strip. The two halves earned the nickname 'the earmuffs'. Luis Gutiérrez won the seat in 1992; a 1996 report put the district at about 65 percent Hispanic.

title: Louisiana's Z-shaped 4th
text: Louisiana's 1992 map added a second majority-Black district, the 4th, a 'Z-shaped creature' that zigzagged through all or part of 28 parishes and five of the state's largest cities. Cleo Fields won it in 1992. A federal court struck it down as a racial gerrymander in Hays v. Louisiana (1993), and the state redrew it in 1994.

title: Georgia's 11th and Miller v. Johnson
text: Georgia's third majority-Black district joined Black neighborhoods in metro Atlanta with Black communities in Savannah, population centers the Supreme Court described as '260 miles apart in distance and worlds apart in culture'. In Miller v. Johnson (1995) the Court held that race was the predominant factor in drawing it and that the plan violated the Equal Protection Clause.

title: Texas' 30th and Bush v. Vera
text: The 1991 map's 30th district, in Dallas, was one of three new majority-minority districts, with the 18th and 29th in Houston, that a federal court held to be unconstitutional racial gerrymanders. In Bush v. Vera (1996) the Supreme Court affirmed, finding that race had predominated over traditional districting principles in drawing them.

title: Texas redraws mid-decade
text: After the 2002 election, held under a court-drawn map, Democrats held 17 of Texas' 32 seats. In 2003, at the urging of U.S. House Majority Leader Tom DeLay, the Republican legislature drew a new map; Democratic legislators twice broke quorum, fleeing to Ardmore, Oklahoma, and Albuquerque, New Mexico. Under the new map Republicans won 21 of the 32 seats in 2004.

title: The 'fajita strip'
text: The 2003 map's 25th district, nicknamed the 'fajita strip', ran from McAllen and the Mexican border to Austin. The Supreme Court in LULAC v. Perry described it as 'a long, narrow strip' with 'a 300-mile gap between the Latino communities' it joined. Democrat Lloyd Doggett won it in 2004.

title: Texas' 23rd and LULAC v. Perry
text: As Latino voters in the 23rd turned against incumbent Henry Bonilla, the 2003 map split Webb County and Laredo, moving about 100,000 Latinos into District 28 and cutting the 23rd's Latino citizen voting-age share from 57.5 percent to 46 percent. In LULAC v. Perry (2006) the Supreme Court held that District 23 violated Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, while leaving most of the 2003 map in place.

title: Pennsylvania's 7th: 'Goofy kicking Donald Duck'
text: The 2011 map's 7th district wound through Delaware, Montgomery, Chester, Berks and Lancaster counties. In one place along Route 30 it stayed contiguous only through a medical facility's grounds, and in King of Prussia through a single steak and seafood restaurant. Its outline earned the nickname 'Goofy kicking Donald Duck'.

title: Maryland's 3rd: the 'broken-winged pterodactyl'
text: Upholding Maryland's 2011 map in Fletcher v. Lamone, Judge Paul Niemeyer wrote that the 3rd district was 'reminiscent of a broken-winged pterodactyl, lying prostrate across the center of the State'. A 2012 analysis by Azavea ranked it the least compact district in the country on two of four standard measures.

title: Ohio's 9th: the 'snake by the lake'
text: Ohio's 2011 map stretched the 9th along Lake Erie from west of Toledo to Cleveland; at one point it was only as wide as a beach. The map put Democratic incumbents Marcy Kaptur and Dennis Kucinich in the same district, and Kaptur won their March 2012 primary.

title: North Carolina's 12th again: Cooper v. Harris
text: North Carolina's 2011 map kept the 12th as a thin band along Interstate 85, joining parts of Charlotte and Greensboro with an arm reaching Winston-Salem. In Cooper v. Harris (May 22, 2017) the Supreme Court held that the 1st and 12th districts were racial gerrymanders.

title: Florida's 5th and the Fair Districts amendment
text: Florida's 5th district ran from Jacksonville to Orlando. In July 2015 the Florida Supreme Court held that it, along with seven other districts, violated the state's Fair Districts amendment, and ordered it redrawn east-west. From 2016 it ran from Jacksonville west along the Georgia border past Tallahassee.

title: Pennsylvania's 2011 map struck down
text: In three elections under the 2011 map, Republicans won the same 13 of Pennsylvania's 18 districts and Democrats the same five. On January 22, 2018, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court held the map 'clearly, plainly and palpably' violated the state constitution, later explaining that it violated the Free and Equal Elections Clause. The 2011 plan split 28 counties.

title: Pennsylvania's court-drawn map
text: The Pennsylvania Supreme Court adopted its own remedial map on February 19, 2018. It split 13 counties, compared with 28 under the 2011 plan. In the 2018 election under the new map, Democrats and Republicans each won nine seats.

title: Allen v. Milligan
text: Alabama's 2021 map had one majority-Black district (the 7th) out of seven. A federal court found it likely violated Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, but the Supreme Court stayed that ruling, so this map was used in 2022. On June 8, 2023, the Court affirmed the lower court 5 to 4 in Allen v. Milligan.

title: Alabama's court-drawn 2nd
text: After the legislature's 2023 map again had only one majority-Black district, a federal court adopted a special master's map in October 2023. Its 2nd district ran from Mobile County across the southern Black Belt with a Black voting-age population of 48.7 percent, and Democrat Shomari Figures won it in 2024. On June 2, 2026, the Supreme Court allowed Alabama to return to its 2023 legislative map.

title: Louisiana's second majority-Black district
text: In January 2024 Louisiana enacted a map (SB8) with a second majority-Black district, the 6th, running from Shreveport to Baton Rouge; Democrat Cleo Fields won it in 2024. In Louisiana v. Callais (April 29, 2026), the Supreme Court held 6 to 3 that the Voting Rights Act did not require the district, making it an unconstitutional racial gerrymander. Louisiana enacted a new map in 2026 that eliminated it.
